item.title: Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/ckz7z5w7ey2jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious - Published An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage. That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians. But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza. And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia. No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis. So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football? Venue changes have not quietened protests As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza. In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag. The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott. Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income. As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures. No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary. Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly. The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin. The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest. In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years. The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition. Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean. FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide". "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel." In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity". The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations". Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN). In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice. The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers. On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population." Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide. The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football. In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen. The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned. In a statement released on Tuesday, Amnesty International said Uefa was "giving Israel an international stage" rather than "sending a clear message there is a cost" for its actions in Gaza. BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations. But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October. Related topics - Published7 hours ago

item.title: What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dx5dy5rzz2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump? - Published When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event. This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news – the White House Press pool. Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications, as well as potentially affecting coverage of the future presidential engagements. Tensions are high. During Trump's visit to the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, he lashed out at a reporter from CNN - one of the media outlets he has come into conflict with. What is the White House press pool? It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday. There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category. The idea, conceived decades ago, is that having a pool saves on costs and space and it is not practical for hundreds of media outlets to follow the president around. Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media. The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation. This latest row centres on the TV pool which has five members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC. It began on Friday when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team. A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled. On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events. That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House. With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks. But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there. Why did US networks pull out of filming Trump? Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC on Monday that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump. In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. "No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting." The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms. It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage. CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday. In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday was unaffected by the boycott because it was carried by outlets which are not part of the pool. But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout. CNN appears to have taken the decision not to run Trump's UN speech live, despite it being made available through official UN sources. It should have been the pool news outlet with the president on Tuesday but is no longer travelling with him since his ban. CNN Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins still attended the UN meetings, where she asked him a question as he spoke to reporters. "I'm surprised CNN is here covering me… you should not be here covering me," Trump said, singling out Collins, whom he has frequently criticised and insulted in the past. She responded by pointing out that the UN, not the White House, accredits journalists to cover the General Assembly. How has Trump reacted and what is Trump TV? Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements. "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube. Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies. For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York. Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience. Have there been previous examples of White House media bans? In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access. The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009. But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview. item.title: Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's 2020 death case has been reopened
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpwl1ejlgw9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's 2020 death case has been reopened - Published On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel. She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration. As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days. It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive. On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead. Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai. Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally. Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide. But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death. The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered. His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years. In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years. The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers". They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall. "We find this difficult to accept," they wrote. One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime. Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him. The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case. Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput. "She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added. Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote. In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home. Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment. But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues. Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death. In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked. Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain. "In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused." In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them". But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta. Satish Salian, who's been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter, says he's felt "some peace" after the court ordered the fresh investigation into her death. Disha, he told the BBC, was "very bright, she did well in her studies and read a lot. She had a heart of gold and was very helpful. She was our only child and she loved us very much". His wife, he says, has been unable to come to terms with her tragic death and has gone into depression. "I want the death penalty for those who hurt my daughter. Those who inflicted pain on her must die a painful death too. That is what justice for Disha would look like to me," he says.

Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after Iran-backed Houthis seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. Now, following a Saudi request, the UK has said it will deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jets taking part in "purely defensive" missions. The BBC's Frank Gardner has this analysis.
